```{r load-lib, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(readr)
library(tidymodels)


```


```{r}
#Read the data and read it with the correct delimiter
communities_df <- read.csv("data/communities.data")

#Cleaning up the data frame, converting "?" to NA

#Major issues with just reading this data as it is. The variable names are actually an observation for "Lakewood city". There are 2 solutions: 1) go through, one by one and rename all the variable names, or 2) figure out someway to restore the variable names.

#After inspection, it does not seem like the variable names are stored in the data set. I also am not sure which headings go where in the data. So fun...

communities_heading_df <- read.csv("data/communities_heading.data")

#time to clean up NA values and figure out what the data even means.

communities_clean_df <- communities_heading_df %>%
  mutate(
    across(where(is.character), ~na_if(., "?")),
    across(where(is.character) & !c(communityname.string), ~as.numeric(.x))
  )

communities_clean_df <- communities_clean_df[, colMeans(is.na(communities_clean_df)) <= 0.5]

```

```{r}
#lets see some summary statistics of the data. Lets check the mean.
#More of these statisitcs can be found in the "data/communities.names".

summary_stat_communities <- communities_clean_df |> 
  select(-communityname.string) |> 
  summarise(
    across(everything(),
    ~ round(mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 2))
  ) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Mean"
  )

#Now we can see which columns have missing values, and how many.
communities_clean_df |> 
  mutate(
    across(everything(), ~ is.na(.))
  ) |> 
  colSums()

```

```{r}
#Values presented in this table are "normalised" from 0 to 1. A normalised value represents where a value sits on the range. e.g: A value of 0 represents the min/smallest population, while a value of 1 represents the largest population.

#It also needs to be pivoted longer, while the "clean" data looks clean, its not fully clean. we will insert a categorical variable. We will also remove the first 3 variables and fold variable, as it is unsure how they add to the data in a meaningful way.


community_long <-   communities_heading_df |> 
  mutate(
    across(where(is.character), ~na_if(., "?")),
    across(where(is.character) & !c(communityname.string), ~as.numeric(.x))
  ) |> 
  select(-state.numeric,-county.numeric,-community.numeric,-fold.numeric) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(population.numeric:PolicBudgPerPop.numeric),
    values_to = "NormalisedValue",
    names_to = "Category"
  )

```

```{r}
#lets take a look at any correlation between variables.

community_long |>
  filter(Category == "medIncome.numeric") |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x=NormalisedValue,
      y=ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric,
    )
  )+
  geom_bin_2d(bins=20)+
  geom_smooth(method = lm,
              se = TRUE,
              colour = "red")+
  theme_bw()+
  labs(
    x = "Median Income",
    y = "Violent Crimes per Population"
  )


#The correlation for each variable should be calculated as well. Might write a function to calculate these values and store them in a matrix. yay...

#lets check if there is already a correlation function.

```

```{r}
#Lets calculate the correlation between median income and violent crime per pop.
cor(communities_clean_df$medIncome.numeric,communities_clean_df$ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric)

#Can a column be made describing the correlation between all the other numeric variables with respect to violent crimes per population.

community_long |> 
  group_by(Category) |> 
  mutate(CorWViolCim = cor(NormalisedValue,ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric))

#this works but the number of decimal points are messy, lets round it to 3 decimal places.

#community_long <- community_long |> 
  #group_by(Category) |> 
  #mutate(CorWViolCim = round(cor(NormalisedValue,ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric), digits = 3))

#This does work but there are so many repeated values and observations, it should probably be made into another table for easier reading. Readings also range from -1 to 1, so a magnitude of the correlation should be taken to determine which variables are most correlated with "Violent Crimes" per population.

community_CorWVilCrim <- community_long |> 
  drop_na(NormalisedValue) |> 
  group_by(Category) |> 
  mutate(CorWViolCrim = round(cor(NormalisedValue,ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric), digits = 3)) |>
  mutate(MagCorWVilCrim = sqrt(CorWViolCrim^2)) |> 
  select(Category,CorWViolCrim,MagCorWVilCrim) |> 
  unique()

#What would also be useful is to maybe see if there are correlations between variables. A good way to do this might be to turn the data into some kind of "matrix" of correlation values. It is also worth noting that the correlation value for something correlated with itself is '1'.

cor(communities_clean_df$population.numeric,communities_clean_df$population.numeric) #this returns '1'

#This will also be a symmetrical matrix.

```

```{r}
#Each observation needs to be given some kind of ID

X1 <-communities_heading_df |> 
  mutate(
    across(where(is.character), ~na_if(., "?")),
    across(where(is.character) & !c(communityname.string), ~as.numeric(.x)),
    ID = seq_len(nrow(communities_heading_df))
    ) |> 
  select(-communityname.string,-state.numeric,-county.numeric,-community.numeric,-fold.numeric)


Y1 <- communities_heading_df |> 
  mutate(
    across(where(is.character), ~na_if(., "?")),
    across(where(is.character) & !c(communityname.string), ~as.numeric(.x)),
    ID = seq_len(nrow(communities_heading_df))
    ) |> 
  select(-communityname.string,-state.numeric,-county.numeric,-community.numeric,-fold.numeric) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(population.numeric:ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric),
    values_to = "NormalisedValue",
    names_to = "Category"
  )

#Matrix_values <- full_join(Y1,X1) |> 
  #group_by(Category) |> 
  #mutate(
    #across(
      #c(population.numeric:ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric), ~round(cor(NormalisedValue,., use = "complete.obs"), digits = 3)
    #)
  #) |> 
  #select(-NormalisedValue,-ID) |> 
  #unique()

#Issue with this result, there are a few bands of just "NA" results. Maybe a better join could be used instead of full_join?
#The solution was to instead add 'use = "complete.obs"' as this only did calculations when there were 2 values in both vectors.

#This can also be cleaned up. and turned into 3 columns: an X1, Y1, and correlation value.

Cor_Values <- full_join(Y1,X1) |> 
  group_by(Category) |> 
  mutate(
    across(
      c(population.numeric:ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric), ~round(cor(NormalisedValue,., use = "complete.obs"), digits = 3)
    )
  ) |> 
  select(-NormalisedValue,-ID) |> 
  unique() |> 
  rename("X1" = "Category") |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(population.numeric:ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric),
    names_to = "Y1",
    values_to = "Correlation"
  )
```

```{r}

#The correlations between each column and the violent crime column can be calculated. (the absolute value is taken because the strenth of the correlation will be compared, and as such whether it is negative or positive does not matter)

community_corr_ranked <- community_long %>%
  drop_na(NormalisedValue) %>%
  group_by(Category) %>%
  summarise(
    r = cor(NormalisedValue, ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric),
    abs_r = abs(r)
  ) %>%
  filter(Category != "ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric") %>%
  arrange(desc(abs_r)) %>%
  filter(Category != "ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric") %>%
  filter(abs_r >= 0.5) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs_r))

#

ggplot(community_corr_ranked, aes(x = r, y = reorder(Category, r), fill = r > 0)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("cadetblue3", "indianred3")) +
  labs(
    title = "Top Correlates with Violent Crime (|r| >= 0.5)",
    subtitle = "Positive (coral) vs Negative (blue) Pearson correlation coefficients",
    x = "Correlation Coefficient (r)",
    y = "Community Characteristic"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

```


```{r}
#look into modeling
linear_reg() |> 
  set_engine("lm") |> 
  fit(ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric ~ medIncome.numeric, data = communities_clean_df)

#consider a new model with MedIncome and PctUnemployed as explanatory variables. How does that change the original coefficients?

linear_reg() |> 
  set_engine("lm") |> 
  fit(ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric ~ medIncome.numeric+PctUnemployed.numeric, data = communities_clean_df)

#Question: Is the model a better estimator if the intercept approaches 0?

linear_reg() |> 
  set_engine("lm") |> 
  fit(ViolentCrimesPerPop.numeric ~ medIncome.numeric+PctUnemployed.numeric+PctPopUnderPov.numeric, data = communities_clean_df)

#Note: with the addition of PctUnemployed and PctPopUnderPov, the coefficient for MedIncome has approached 0.

#Initial guess is that MedIncome is not the best estimator, and that a MedIncomes effects on ViolentCrimesPerPop was quite dependent on and correlated with these other 2 variables.
```
